quick_notes.title: Constitution Recap
quick_notes.explanation: Title: Constitution Recap The Indian Constitution borrowed ideas from other countries, like the United States (USA) for the system of a written constitution and fundamental rights, and the United Kingdom (UK) for the parliamentary system of government. The 42nd Amendment, passed in 1976, is often called the "Mini-Constitution" because it made many major changes, including adding the words "Socialist" and "Secular" to the Preamble. The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists the official languages of India, such as Hindi, Bengali, and Tamil, and currently includes 22 languages. The Tenth Schedule, also known as the anti-defection law, lays down rules to stop elected members of Parliament or state legislatures from switching political parties, and if they do, they can be disqualified from their seat.

quick_notes.title: Rights Recap
quick_notes.explanation: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution completely bans the practice of untouchability, which is the unfair treatment of people based on their caste. Article 32 gives every person the right to go directly to the Supreme Court if their Fundamental Rights are violated, and this article is called the heart and soul of the Constitution because it makes those rights enforceable. Article 51A lists the Fundamental Duties of every Indian citizen, such as respecting the national flag and protecting the environment. Article 44, which is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy, says the state should work toward having a Uniform Civil Code (UCC), meaning a single set of personal laws for all citizens regardless of their religion.

quick_notes.title: Executive Recap
quick_notes.detail: President (35 age/72 Pardon). PM (Real head). Governor (Nominal state). TN Assembly (234 seats/Unicameral).
quick_notes.explanation: The President of India must be at least 35 years old and has the power to grant pardons under Article 72 of the Constitution. The Prime Minister is the real head of the government, meaning they lead the country's actual day-to-day administration. The Governor is the nominal or ceremonial head of a state, representing the central government there. The Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly has 234 seats and is unicameral, which means it has only one chamber or house for making laws, unlike some states that have two houses.

quick_notes.title: Local Gov Recap
quick_notes.explanation: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, passed in 1992, gave constitutional status to local self-government in India. The 73rd Amendment deals with Panchayats (village-level councils) and the 74th Amendment deals with Municipalities (urban local bodies). A committee headed by Balwant Rai Mehta recommended a three-tier system of Panchayati Raj, meaning three levels of rural local government: village, block, and district. Article 243 of the Constitution contains the provisions for Panchayats, including their powers, composition, and elections. The 73rd Amendment originally required that at least one-third of all seats in Panchayats be reserved for women. In Tamil Nadu

quick_notes.title: Institutions Recap
quick_notes.explanation: Article 324 of the Constitution establishes the Election Commission, which is the independent body that conducts free and fair elections in India. Article 148 creates the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General, or CAG, who audits all government accounts to ensure public money is spent properly. Article 315 provides for a Public Service Commission, or PSC, at the national level and for each state; these commissions recruit civil servants through competitive exams. The Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission, or TNPSC, was established in 1929 and is the state-level PSC that recruits for Tamil Nadu government jobs. Article 280 sets up the Finance Commission, or FC, which recommends how tax money should be shared between the central government and the states.
